paragraphs.heading: The end of an era
paragraphs.text: The Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction, shortened to K–Pg and once called the K–T extinction, wiped out about three-quarters of the plant and animal species on Earth around 65.5 million years ago. It killed the dinosaurs, along with most other tetrapods that weighed over 25 kg, with a few exceptions such as sea turtles and crocodilians. The event closed both the Cretaceous period and the Mesozoic era. It also opened the Cenozoic, the era we still live in today.

paragraphs.heading: A clue in the rocks
paragraphs.text: In rocks formed both on land and under the sea, all around the world, the event shows up as a thin band of sediment known as the K–Pg boundary. The clay in that layer holds unusually high amounts of iridium, a metal that is more common in asteroids than in Earth's crust. The idea that an asteroid caused the extinction is known as the impact hypothesis, or the Alvarez hypothesis. It got strong backing in the early 1990s, when a crater 180 km across, named Chicxulub, was found on the Yucatán Peninsula in the Gulf of Mexico.

paragraphs.heading: How the impact killed
paragraphs.text: Most scientists think the asteroid was 10 to 15 km wide. The worst damage probably came from a lingering impact winter that halted photosynthesis in plants and plankton, as particles in the air blocked sunlight from reaching the ground. Drilling into the crater in 2016 found granite flung up within minutes from deep inside the Earth, but hardly any gypsum, the sulfate-bearing sea floor rock usual in that region. That missing gypsum would have turned to vapour and spread through the air as an aerosol, with longer-term effects on climate and the food chain. In 2019, researchers also argued that the impact quickly made the oceans more acidic.

paragraphs.heading: Other suspects
paragraphs.text: Other possible causes or helpers have been put forward, including volcanic eruptions such as the Deccan Traps, a changing climate and shifts in sea level. Yet in 2020, scientists found that climate models of the extinction favoured the asteroid over volcanism. The timing of the layer of thrown-out material is one line of evidence. Another is that the ecological patterns seen in fossils match modelled disruptions such as darkness and cooling. Together these support the view that the Chicxulub impact set off the die-off.

paragraphs.heading: Who died and who survived
paragraphs.text: On land the victims included the non-avian dinosaurs, every pterosaur, and many mammals, birds, lizards, insects and plants. In the sea, plesiosaurs and mosasaurs vanished, ammonites and rudists died out, and teleost fish, sharks and plankton suffered badly. The mammals and birds that made it through ate insects, worms and snails, which themselves fed on dead plant and animal matter, and no strictly plant-eating or strictly meat-eating mammals seem to have survived. Rivers and lakes lost few animal groups, because their food webs leaned on debris washed in from land more than on living plants. In the oceans, animals of the open water fared worse than those on the sea floor, which could feed on such debris.

paragraphs.heading: A world remade
paragraphs.text: The losses also opened doors. Many groups went through adaptive radiation, a sudden burst into new forms and species that filled the emptied niches. Mammals in particular branched out in the Paleogene Period that followed, giving rise to horses, whales, bats and primates. The only dinosaurs to survive were birds, a few kinds of ground and water fowl, and they radiated into all of today's bird species. Even so, biodiversity took a long time to recover, despite all the empty niches waiting to be filled.
